##段落
给我解释一下：是什么让一首歌“扑街”？从德雷克到凯蒂·佩里，有时候一首歌就是火不起来。作者：琼奎琳·希尔，2026年8月30日，中午12:00（UTC）赠阅。德雷克于2025年在伦敦无线音乐节上登台演出。图片来源：西蒙娜·乔伊纳/盖蒂图片社，供ABA使用。琼奎琳·希尔是《给我解释一下》的主持人，这是你解答所有未解之谜的热线。她于2022年加入Vox，担任高级制作人，随后成为Vox政策播客《The Weeds》的主持人。

##段落
目前有不少音乐人正处于他们的“扑街时代”。想想看：自从2024年与肯德里克·拉马尔的那场骂战中败下阵来后，德雷克就大不如前了。凯蒂·佩里曾一度称霸排行榜，但她最近的发行作品却不再是“烟火”般耀眼。还有那么一个时期，你走进任何一间健身课教室，几乎不可能不听到莉佐的歌，但她最新的专辑却悄无声息地熄火了。换句话说，有些例子是显而易见的。但一首歌“扑街”到底意味着什么？据StereoGum执行主编、著有《榜首金曲：二十首揭示流行音乐史的冠军单曲》一书的汤姆·布雷汉说，这完全是相对而言的。“Spotify上有上百万首歌永远不会有人听到，”他告诉Vox，“这些歌不一定算扑街，因为它们本来就不带什么期望。当一位大牌艺人没能达到自己、粉丝或唱片公司设定的某个基准时，那就很尴尬了。人们就爱抓住这种尴尬，然后大做文章。”

##段落
为什么有些歌一败涂地，而另一些却大获成功？艺人又如何从这些未达预期的落差中翻身？我们在本周的《给我解释一下》节目中探讨了这些问题以及更多内容，这是Vox每周一期的听众来电播客。以下是我与布雷汉对话的节选，经过删减以保持简洁清晰。你可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或任何你收听播客的平台上收听完整节目。如果你想提交问题，请发送邮件至askvox@vox.com或拨打1-800-618-8545。

##段落
扑街的歌是不是就是烂歌？这就是它们扑街的原因吗？在某些情况下，是的。你确实能挑出几首，然后说：“这首不行。”但很多时候，这纯粹是时机和运气的问题。有时候，一位艺人恰好在对的时机出现，积累了口碑，然后推出了适合自己的那首歌。有时候，他们以极其刺耳、明显到让人尴尬的方式误判了风向，结果就是成绩不佳。这种事发生在很多优秀的人身上。不少明星都从扑街中翻过身来，但这种事确实会发生。

##段落
有没有一些其实很棒却扑街的歌？作为一名网络独立音乐评论人，我最典型的例子是卡莉·蕾·杰普森的《Emotion》。她曾凭借《Call Me Maybe》这首歌在全球取得了巨大的突破性成功。她在那之后推出的专辑，是一部精彩、层次丰富、出色的——

##段落
一首流行唱片，我认为它对“你可以是一位既是流行明星又是小众艺术家”的观念产生了影响，就像独立摇滚乐队或地下说唱歌手那样。但它销量不佳，数字不漂亮。所以在当时，它是一张备受评论界喜爱却商业失败的唱片。一首歌成为热门，有多少取决于音乐本身，又有多少取决于病毒式传播和营销？这两者紧密相连。很多时候，艺术家们制作歌曲是为了走红，或者制作歌曲来评论自己的公众形象。当像Lizzo这样的人推出了一张表现不佳的唱片，这就不再仅仅是“哦，人们不喜欢这首歌”的故事，而变成了“哦，人们不喜欢这个人”或“这个人已经耗尽了善意”。比如Lizzo的一首歌：无论歌曲成功与否，你都能听到她的个性从扬声器中跳跃出来。所以歌曲和艺术家变得密不可分，歌曲和营销也变得密不可分。还有一个艺术家从巅峰跌至谷底的例子，我很想深入探讨，那就是Katy Perry。我觉得我们已经远离了超级碗上的Left Shark时代。发生了什么？Katy Perry经历了过去流行明星才有的职业生涯，那段时期她疯狂主导，接二连三地推出热门歌曲，势不可挡。然后一切随时间逐渐消退。一张专辑有五首冠军单曲，下一张有两首，再下一张根本没有重大热门，只有几首前十。她在疫情刚开始时发行了一张专辑。你可以说：“那张没做好，不是她的错。”然后她长期担任《美国偶像》评委，长期在拉斯维加斯驻唱。接着她说：“够了。我退出《美国偶像》。我要回归，成为你们想要的那个流行明星。”她做了一张糟糕的专辑。她还与Dr. Luke重聚，后者曾是她许多大热歌曲的联合创作者和制作人，但自从她停止与他合作以来，就有指控出现。Kesha，这位在Katy Perry出道时曾是朋友的人，正是提出这些指控的人。所以互联网有很多可以炒作的点。“尤其是现在，一首歌可以基于流量和讨论首次亮相就登顶第一，然后从排行榜上消失。”这就是一首歌从糟糕歌曲变成臭名昭著的失败之作的方式——不仅歌曲表现不佳，还实际上烧掉了这个人积累的大量善意。有哪些歌曲是大家原本期待大爆，结果却惨败的？一首歌有可能成为冠军单曲却仍然是失败之作。尤其是现在，一首歌可以首秀就登顶。

在流媒体和话题度上排名第一，然后它就可能从榜单上消失。1996年，迈克尔·杰克逊发行了《You Are Not Alone》。这首歌首周空降第一名，但很快就跌落了。专辑销量不佳，这首歌最终也没被记住多少，多年来确实进入了臭名昭著的“阴影地带”。有没有例子是歌曲最初被乐评人讨厌，但后来成为经典的？太多了。那些当时是热门歌曲、却被普遍认为烦人的歌，成功率很高。人们曾被汉森的《MMMBop》或辣妹组合的《Wannabe》惹恼。当ABBA走红时，确实有乐评人理解他们，但我想说，他们当时被广泛视为笑柄。现在，那只是无可挑剔、美丽、有影响力的流行音乐目录。像Quad City DJ's的《C'mon N' Ride It (The Train)》在1990年代并不是乐评人争相称赞的歌曲，但作为一个当时的孩子，我可以告诉你，那首歌一直很带劲，而且从未停止过。人们对流行音乐成功最大的误解是什么？我认为最大的误解是认为唱片公司或企业可以策划出一个巨无霸热门。他们可以观察趋势，可以把钱投入到推广中，但你永远不知道人们真正会抓住什么、不会抓住什么。他们可以做些事情来制造某种东西正在走红的假象，但你需要真正的持续成功，才能让所有人都说：“好吧，不，这确实很火。”如果艺人进入了“失败期”，他们通常如何回应？有一段辉煌的、美丽的历史，许多艺人不反复尝试同样的东西，而是转为幕后人物。他们为别人写歌，或做制作人，或成为经理人。Max Martin，现在在拥有冠军单曲的作曲家中领先于约翰·列侬，但落后于保罗·麦卡特尼，他在80年代是一个瑞典乐队的主唱，试图成为邦·乔维，但从未走红。他的乐队叫It's Alive。你可以上网听听他们的歌。它们不是很好，但他最终与各种不同的人合作，做出了这些不可思议的唱片。这样的情况很多。在流行音乐史上，这种情况发生了无数次。这当然是应对失败问题的一种方式。查看更多：文化 向我解释 音乐 播客 最高法院最糟糕的想法之一可能在中期选举中拯救特朗普 一首关于德克萨斯州的悲伤乡村歌曲可能成为史上最热门的歌曲 播客 用最新的Vox填字游戏休息一下脑筋 总统候选人成功戏弄特朗普的白宫 播客 Zohran Mamdani如何卷入印度教民族主义的争斗 邮件

readings.title: The overlooked benefits of laughing at yourself
body: 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Laurie Clarke Research shows it's sometimes good for us to poke fun at ourselves, but not always. Here's how to harness the benefits, while avoiding the pitfalls. Why do some schoolchildren become outcasts? In the 1990s, psychologists set out to investigate why some kids were excluded by their peers. They discovered two archetypes. Some of the rejected children were bullying and aggressive. Others were meek and subservient. Both shared one quality: an inability to take a joke .  The first group was responded to teasing with anger or violence, while the second felt wounded and withdrew. Both interpreted the intended humour as an insult, something that couldn't possibly be in good faith. More socially assured kids, on the other hand, shrugged off teasing, or were amused by it. Whether we can laugh at ourselves can clearly have consequences from an early age.  Studies show that throughout life, a more light-hearted and humorous outlook on life is better for your mental health, relationships and overall prospects. Still, opinion on whether it is a good idea to laugh at yourself specifically has long been divided. Now, though, researchers are finally beginning to understand the nuance of what it really means to poke fun at ourselves – and when and how it might be beneficial. Is it even possible to laugh at yourself? Plato didn't think so. The Ancient Greek philosopher believed that humour was triggered by feeling superior to others – particularly those who delusionally believe they are better-looking or wiser than they really are. If you really hate people laughing at you, you could be a gelotophobe – someone with an acute sensitivity to laughter More than 1,000 years later, in 1651, English philosopher Thomas Hobbes largely agreed . The exception – when people were occasionally able to laugh at themselves – was when reflecting on a past foolishness, which demonstrated how much worldlier they had become in the interim. Eventually, philosophers began to allow that not all humour was motivated by spite. In the 18th Century, for example, the popular "incongruity theory" proposed that hilarity often results from an unexpected violation of social norms. Still, whether people can actually laugh at themselves remained a contentious topic right up until recent times. Most humour research from the past 50 years has relied on asking people if they can laugh at themselves and taking their word for it. But like the weekly units of alcohol people confess to on doctors' forms, there was a possibility that the reports were a little aspirational. Perhaps people weren't quite as sporting as they claimed. In 2011, though, European researchers tested the ability using an experimental set-up instead. They invited test subjects into the lab and covertly videotaped their faces. When they next came in, the subjects were presented with distorted, fun-house mirror style images of their faces, and their reactions were recorded. Not everyone was amused, but 80% at least smiled when unexpectedly encountering the image. Forty per cent were extra tickled and laughed aloud. "Now the science is quite settled that yes, it is possible to laugh at oneself, and there are actually quite numerous benefits associated with that," says Sonja Heintz, a lecturer in psychology at Plymouth University, UK, who researches humour. Being able to laugh at yourself is one of the most challenging types of humour to master, claimed influential American humour researcher Paul McGhee in 2010. In McGhee's seven-step humour programme (targeted at those suffering "terminal seriousness" like Plato), learning to laugh at oneself was the penultimate step – second only in difficulty to "finding humour in stressful situations."  McGhee saw laughing at yourself as the gateway to other types of humour; a "core component" of a more mirthful existence. "Because if someone takes themselves very seriously, it's difficult to engage in humour in general," explains Heintz.   Some find self-mockery easier to master than others. If you really hate people laughing at you, you could be a gelotophobe – someone with an acute sensitivity to laughter. "You might be sitting in a cafe and joking with your friends, and someone might approach you and ask, why did you laugh at me?" says René Proyer, psychology professor at Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Germany. For gelotophobes, even a smile can indicate their interlocutor thinks them a ridiculous person.  There is no one factor explaining why one might become a gelotophobe, but Proyer says that a very strict and punishing style of parenting is one risk factor . Another is an early traumatic experience of having been laughed at. "So a really embarrassing situation at school, for example," says Proyer, "where you are the butt of jokes for weeks, months, perhaps years." Autism appears to be another risk factor . There also seems to be a cultural dimension. East Asian countries generally have higher levels of gelotophobia than Western nations, something researchers attribute to those belonging to collectivistic cultures being less likely to single themselves out for attention, or to engage in humour as a coping mechanism. These cultures tend to believe humour is best left to the professionals. In China, for example, people are more likely to associate humour with "experts", i.e. comedians, than everyday citizens. Like the children unable to take teasing, gelotophobes tend to experience worse psychological and interpersonal outcomes. The trait has been tied to lower life satisfaction, greater friendship avoidance, and increased loneliness and depression. The opposite trait is gelotophilia, the joy of being laughed at by others, which has been linked to stronger social connectedness. One way this can manifest is in "playfulness", the tendency to take oneself and the world lightly. "Playful people are able to frame or reframe everyday situations in a way such that they experience them as entertaining or intellectually stimulating or personally interesting," says Proyer. "A highly playful person is able to do a boring task or chore and reframe it in a way that is somewhat amusing." Research has established playfulness as a predictor of higher self-esteem and relationship satisfaction .  Most experts agree that humour is beneficial to our relationships. But the kind of humour matters too.  In 2003, Canadian researchers developed the Humor Styles Questionnaire , which divides people's dominant humour type into four categories: affiliative humour, self-enhancing humour, aggressive humour and self-defeating humour.  The questionnaire soon became hugely influential. "It was the first time anyone had considered that humour could be adaptive but also maladaptive," says Claire Fox, professor of psychology of education at the University of Bristol, UK.  Self-enhancing humourists are attuned to the fragile absurdities of humanity and existence. They agree with statements like: "If I am feeling upset or unhappy I usually try to think of something funny about the situation to make myself feel better". These individuals make light of their problems as a coping mechanism. This was seen as an adaptive humour type. "Self-defeating" humour, on the other hand, was thought to be maladaptive. Self-defeating humourists agree with statements like: "I often try to make people like or accept me more by saying something funny about my own weaknesses, blunders, or faults." At the time, this type of humour was seen as signalling neediness and low self-esteem. When Heintz first began researching humour in the 2010s, she was taken aback to find that poking fun at oneself was viewed so negatively by the field. "Because my personal humour style is [that] I make fun of myself all the time," she says. "I don't take myself seriously." Reading the literature, Heintz was surprised to find that someone like her was supposedly at higher risk of anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation. To find out if self-defeatists really were all that self-loathing, Heintz rounded up a group of them and compared them to those with other humour styles. If the predominant thinking was correct, "these people should really suffer with mental health issues", says Heintz. But not a single one did. On the contrary, she found that self-defeating humour was associated with higher levels of self-esteem and better interpersonal relationships. "They all said, 'Well, I struggle a bit with self-esteem. I'm a bit insecure. But making fun of myself is actually a really good way for me to cope with these difficulties, and it gives me a way to connect with others'," says Heintz. Most research finding a connection between self-defeating humour and worse mental health and relationship outcomes is correlational , says Heintz, rather than showing a causal effect. Other research has found that the impacts of self-defeating humour can vary across different contexts. A 2014 study by Fox found that schoolchildren who were the victim of bullying used more self-defeating humour than others, and that this preference became more pronounced over time.  But a follow-up study she carried out in 2016 added nuance to the picture. This study labelled kids based on the type of humour they preferred. One group, dubbed the "self-defeaters", engaged only in self-defeating humour. This group seemed to fare worst, ranking the lowest for self-esteem and becoming lonelier over time. But some kids used self-defeating humour even more than the self-defeatists and didn't suffer the same ill effects. The difference was that these kids, dubbed "humour endorsers", engaged in all four different humour types. While those who solely relied on self-defeating humour suffered a social penalty, the humour endorsers did not.  "This suggested that it's actually okay to use self-defeating humour, as long as you're using it in combination with other styles of humour as well," says Fox.  It's not that self-defeating humour never poses an issue. "If you make fun of yourself and it comes from a place of bitterness and self-hatred, then yes, it's probably not good for you," says Heintz. But Heintz now believes that a lot of the negative press around self-defeating humour might  stem from a methodological issue with the Humor Styles Questionnaire. The questions relating to self-defeating humour often introduce a value judgement, she notes, specifying things like: "I do it too much. I do it more than I should."  Could this negative self-judgement be skewing the results? Heintz is now working on a forthcoming paper evaluating 25 years of the questionnaire where she'll propose a rethink of the self-defeating scale. Other researchers are already devising new scales which distinguish between truly self-defeating humour and its more adaptive varieties (like that old British standby, self-deprecating humour). As good comedians know, you should only mock yourself if you've made peace with the flaw or mistake you're making fun of. If you're making a joke from a place of discomfort, people pick up on that and feel awkward, says Heintz. "We need to know that when people make a joke, it's not to be taken seriously. That safety needs to be there for someone to respond to that humour." Moderation is also something to keep in mind. Between self-deprecating and self-defeating humour, "the distinction appears to be about excess and going overboard", says Fox.  Still, it's clear that learning to laugh at yourself can afford psychological and social benefits. Not taking yourself too seriously has been found to help with coping with life's setbacks. Part of this is the simple reason that if you make a mistake, as everyone does from time to time, you're opting for a positive emotional response (laughter) over a negative one (anger or gloom).  "It's related to self-transcendence, which means that when something goes wrong, we can keep that distance from the event and see it a bit more objectively… see the lighter side of things," says Heintz. "We also know that there is a causal effect between things like life satisfaction , coping skills and general well-being." On the interpersonal side, laughing at yourself can be an important tool in your social arsenal. "It's a very safe way to engage in humour in new situations, if you are with strangers and don't quite know their sense of humour yet," says Heintz. When there is a power differential, it can be especially expedient. Another study by Fox found that lecturers engaging in so-called self-defeating humour were seen more positively by students. And those who laugh off minor errors – as long as they do not impact others – are seen as warmer and more competent .    humour So, if you're one of the terminally serious, how can you go about cultivating a lighter attitude towards yourself? McGhee advocated zeroing in on your sore spots – whether it's your height, weight, baldness or clumsiness – and confronting these "no-laugh zones" head-on. However excruciating at first, he promised "a sense of exhilaration and liberation" will follow "as you become comfortable with joking about the things that used to simply annoy or embarrass you."  The first step is admitting to the things you don't like about yourself to others, starting with the most minor. Then start making jokes. "Let's say you're not very interested in fashion, you could poke fun at, 'Oh, I'm wearing the same old jeans again'," says Heintz. "Or, look, I did my shopping at Temu." Eventually, you're ready to make gags about your most agonising insecurities. More like this •  Why performing stand-up is good for your health •  Why do we laugh inappropriately? •  How I changed my personality in six weeks If prodding at your sore spots feels like too much, you could start by cultivating a more amused attitude in general. Proyer carried out a study where he tested whether it was possible to increase playfulness in participants using simple activities over the course of a week. For example, setting aside 10 minutes each evening to write down the three most playful things that happened during the day, "whether this was a thought that you had, or something you observed on your way to work", says Proyer. By and large, the participants perceived themselves as more playful up to three months afterwards – as well as reporting reduced levels of depressiveness and greater happiness.  So what was the most playful thing that happened to you today? Write it down and laugh yourself silly. --  For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  Psychology Mental health Wellbeing Health Comedy Features

16小时前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 Laurie Clarke 研究表明，自嘲有时对我们有好处，但并非总是如此。以下是如何利用其益处，同时避免陷阱。为什么有些学童会成为被排斥的对象？在1990年代，心理学家着手调查为什么有些孩子被同龄人排斥。他们发现了两种典型类型。一些被排斥的孩子表现霸道且具有攻击性。另一些则温顺且服从。两者都有一个共同点：无法接受玩笑。第一组对戏弄的反应是愤怒或暴力，而第二组感到受伤并退缩。两者都将预期的幽默解读为侮辱，认为这不可能是善意的。相比之下，更有社交自信的孩子对戏弄一笑置之，或觉得有趣。我们是否能自嘲，显然从小就会产生影响。研究表明，在整个生命中，对生活持更轻松幽默的态度，对你的心理健康、人际关系和整体前景更好。尽管如此，关于自嘲是否是个好主意，长期以来意见分歧。但现在，研究人员终于开始理解自嘲真正含义的细微差别——以及何时何地可能有益。自嘲甚至可能吗？柏拉图不这么认为。这位古希腊哲学家相信，幽默源于对他人的优越感——特别是对那些妄想自己比实际更漂亮或更聪明的人。如果你真的讨厌别人笑你，你可能是一个“恐笑症”患者——对笑声极度敏感的人。一千多年后，在1651年，英国哲学家托马斯·霍布斯大体同意这一观点。例外情况——当人们偶尔能自嘲时——是在反思过去的愚蠢行为时，这展示了他们在此期间变得多么世故。最终，哲学家们开始承认并非所有幽默都出于恶意。例如，在18世纪，流行的“不协调理论”提出，欢笑常常源于对社会规范的意外违背。尽管如此，人们是否能真正自嘲，直到最近仍是一个有争议的话题。过去50年的大多数幽默研究依赖于询问人们是否能自嘲，并相信他们的说法。但就像人们在医生表格上承认的每周酒精单位一样，这些报告可能有点理想化。也许人们并不像他们声称的那样大度。然而，在2011年，欧洲研究人员改用实验设置来测试这种能力。他们邀请了测试对象——

将受试者带入实验室，秘密录像记录他们的面部表情。当他们再次进入时，受试者被呈现以哈哈镜风格扭曲的自身面部图像，并记录他们的反应。并非所有人都觉得有趣，但80%的人在意外遇到该图像时至少会微笑。40%的人格外被逗乐，并大声笑出来。“现在科学已经相当确定，是的，人们能够自嘲，而且这确实带来了许多益处，”英国普利茅斯大学心理学讲师索尼娅·海因茨说，她研究幽默。能够自嘲是掌握幽默中最具挑战性的类型之一，有影响力的美国幽默研究者保罗·麦吉在2010年声称。在麦吉的七步幽默计划中（针对像柏拉图那样患有“严重严肃症”的人），学会自嘲是倒数第二步——其难度仅次于“在压力情境中寻找幽默”。麦吉将自嘲视为通往其他类型幽默的途径；是更快乐生活的“核心组成部分”。“因为如果某人非常严肃地对待自己，那么总体上很难参与幽默，”海因茨解释道。有些人比其他人更容易掌握自嘲。如果你真的讨厌别人嘲笑你，你可能是个被笑恐惧症患者——对笑声极度敏感的人。“你可能坐在咖啡馆里和朋友开玩笑，有人可能走近你问，你为什么嘲笑我？”德国哈勒-维滕贝格大学心理学教授雷内·普罗耶说。对于被笑恐惧症患者，即使是一个微笑也可能表明他们的对话者认为他们是个可笑的人。没有单一因素能解释为什么一个人会变成被笑恐惧症患者，但普罗耶表示，非常严格和惩罚性的养育风格是一个风险因素。另一个因素是早期被嘲笑的创伤经历。“例如，在学校里一个非常尴尬的情况，”普罗耶说，“你成为笑柄几周、几个月，甚至几年。”自闭症似乎是另一个风险因素。似乎也存在文化维度。东亚国家的被笑恐惧症水平通常高于西方国家，研究人员将其归因于集体主义文化中的人不太可能让自己脱颖而出以吸引注意，或不太可能将幽默作为应对机制。这些文化倾向于认为幽默最好留给专业人士。例如，在中国，人们更可能将幽默与“专家”即喜剧演员联系起来，而不是普通公民。像无法忍受戏弄的孩子一样，被笑恐惧症患者往往经历更差的心理和人际关系结果。这种特质与较低的生活满意度有关。

满意度下降、更多的回避友谊以及孤独感和抑郁情绪的增加。相反的特质是“被笑愉悦”（gelotophilia），即享受被他人取笑的乐趣，这与更强的社会联系有关。这种特质的一种表现是“玩心”（playfulness），即以轻松的态度对待自己和世界。“爱玩的人能够以某种方式重新构建日常情境，使其变得有趣、激发智力或引起个人兴趣，”普罗耶说，“高度爱玩的人能完成枯燥的任务或家务，并以一种有点滑稽的方式重新诠释它。”研究已证实，玩心是更高自尊和关系满意度的预测因素。

##段落

大多数专家同意，幽默对我们的关系有益。但幽默的种类也很重要。2003年，加拿大研究人员开发了“幽默风格问卷”，将人们的主导幽默类型分为四类：亲和型幽默、自我提升型幽默、攻击型幽默和自我贬低型幽默。该问卷迅速产生了巨大影响。“这是第一次有人考虑幽默既可能是适应性的，也可能是适应不良的，”英国布里斯托大学教育心理学教授克莱尔·福克斯说。

##段落

自我提升型幽默者善于察觉人性和存在中脆弱的荒谬之处。他们认同这样的说法：“如果我感到沮丧或不快乐，我通常会试着想些有趣的事情来让自己感觉好一些。”这些人以轻松态度对待自己的问题，作为一种应对机制。这被视为一种适应性幽默类型。另一方面，“自我贬低型”幽默被认为是不适应的。自我贬低型幽默者认同这样的说法：“我经常通过拿自己的弱点、失误或过错开玩笑，来让别人更喜欢或接受我。”当时，这种幽默被视为表现出依赖性和低自尊。

##段落

当海因茨在2010年代开始研究幽默时，她惊讶地发现，该领域对自嘲的评价如此负面。“因为我个人的幽默风格就是一直拿自己开玩笑，”她说，“我不把自己当回事。”阅读文献时，海因茨惊讶地发现，像她这样的人据称有更高的焦虑、抑郁和自杀意念风险。为了弄清自我贬低者是否真的那么自恨，海因茨召集了一组这样的人，并将他们与其他幽默风格的人进行比较。

##段落

如果主流观点是正确的，“这些人应该真的遭受心理健康问题”，海因茨说。但一个也没有。相反，她发现自我贬低型幽默与更高的

##段落
自尊水平更高，人际关系也更融洽。“他们都说，‘嗯，我在自尊方面确实有些挣扎，我有点缺乏安全感。但自嘲实际上是我应对这些困难的一个很好的方式，也给了我一种与他人建立联系的方法，’”海因茨说。海因茨指出，多数发现自嘲式幽默与较差的心理健康和人际关系结果相关联的研究，都是相关性研究，而非证明因果关系。其他研究发现，自嘲式幽默的影响在不同情境下会有所差异。福克斯2014年的一项研究发现，遭受欺凌的学龄儿童比其他人使用更多自嘲式幽默，而且这种偏好随时间推移变得更加明显。但她在2016年进行的后续研究为这一图景增添了细微差别。这项研究根据孩子们偏好的幽默类型给他们贴上了标签。其中一组被称为“自我贬低者”，只使用自嘲式幽默。这一组似乎表现最差，自尊排名最低，并随着时间推移变得更加孤独。但有些孩子使用自嘲式幽默甚至比自我贬低者还多，却没有遭受同样的不良影响。区别在于，这些被称为“幽默支持者”的孩子，会使用所有四种不同类型的幽默。虽然那些只依赖自嘲式幽默的孩子在社交上付出了代价，但幽默支持者却没有。福克斯说：“这表明，只要将自嘲式幽默与其他风格的幽默结合使用，自嘲实际上是可以的。”这并不是说自嘲式幽默永远不会带来问题。“如果你自嘲，而它源于痛苦和自我憎恨，那么是的，它可能对你不好，”海因茨说。但海因茨现在认为，围绕自嘲式幽默的大量负面评价可能源于《幽默风格问卷》在方法论上的一个问题。她指出，与自嘲式幽默相关的问题常常引入价值判断，例如具体说明：“我做得太多了。我做得比应该的要多。”这种负面的自我判断会不会扭曲结果呢？海因茨目前正在撰写一篇即将发表的论文，评估该问卷25年来的使用情况，她将在其中提议重新思考自嘲量表。其他研究人员已经在设计新的量表，以区分真正的自嘲式幽默与其更具适应性的变体（比如英国老牌的自贬式幽默）。正如优秀喜剧演员所知，只有当你已经与所取笑的缺点或错误达成和解时，你才应该自嘲。海因茨说，如果你在感到不适的状态下开玩笑，人们会察觉到并感到尴尬。“我们需要知道，当人们开玩笑时，它并非……”

要认真对待。这种安全感必须存在，人们才会对那种幽默作出回应。”适度也是需要牢记的一点。福克斯表示，在自贬式幽默和自我挫败式幽默之间，“区别似乎在于是否过度和过火”。尽管如此，显然学会自嘲能带来心理和社交上的益处。研究发现，不过于较真有助于应对生活中的挫折。部分原因很简单：如果你犯了错误——每个人都会不时犯错——你选择的是积极情绪反应（笑）而非消极反应（愤怒或沮丧）。海因茨说：“这与自我超越有关，意味着当事情出错时，我们能与该事件保持距离，更客观地看待它……看到事物轻松的一面。我们还知道，生活满意度、应对技能和整体幸福感之间存在因果关系。”在人际交往方面，自嘲可以成为你社交武器库中的重要工具。海因茨说：“这是一种在新环境中安全地参与幽默的方式，如果你和陌生人在一起，还不了解他们的幽默感。”当存在权力差异时，这尤其合适。福克斯的另一项研究发现，使用所谓自我挫败式幽默的讲师在学生眼中更受好评。而那些能一笑而过小错误的人——只要不影响他人——被视为更温暖、更能干。

幽默 所以，如果你是那种极其严肃的人，如何培养对自己更轻松的态度呢？麦吉提倡聚焦你的痛处——无论是身高、体重、秃头还是笨拙——并正面面对这些“禁区”。尽管起初可能令人痛苦，但他承诺，“当你对曾经只是惹恼或让你尴尬的事情开玩笑感到自在时”，会随之而来“一种兴奋和解放的感觉”。第一步是向他人承认你不喜欢自己的地方，从最轻微的开始。然后开始开玩笑。海因茨说：“假设你不太感兴趣时尚，你可以打趣说，‘哦，我又穿这条旧牛仔裤了’。或者，‘看，我在Temu上买了东西’。”最终，你可以准备好对你最痛苦的缺陷开玩笑。更多类似内容 • 为什么表演单口喜剧有益健康 • 我们为什么会不恰当地笑？ • 我如何在六周内改变个性 如果戳痛处感觉太过分，你可以从培养整体上更逗趣的态度开始。普罗耶进行了一项研究，测试是否有可能通过简单的活动来增加参与者的玩心。

一周之内。例如，每天傍晚留出10分钟，记下当天发生的三件最有趣的事情，“无论是你脑海中闪过的一个念头，还是上班路上观察到的一幕，”普罗耶尔说。总的来说，参与者在接下来的三个月里自我感觉更加幽默风趣——同时抑郁感减轻，幸福感增强。那么，今天发生在你身上最有趣的事情是什么呢？写下来，然后尽情大笑吧。——如需获取关于健康与幸福感的专业见解，请订阅由资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写的《健康修复》新闻通讯，她还开设了《更长寿更美好生活》和《迈向平静六步法》课程。欲了解更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。心理学 心理健康 幸福感 健康 喜剧 特写

readings.title: 'Brutal' toll of war on Dubai's tourist trade
body: 2 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sameer Hashmi Last year Dubai welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally, but the US-Israel war with Iran has had a devastating impact on visitor numbers, and local businesses are struggling. On most evenings, Dubai's restaurants would usually be packed, with the constant buzz of diners, of tourists and residents filling tables across the city. But over the past month, many of those tables have sat empty. For Natasha Sideris, the shift has been sudden and stark. She opened her first restaurant in Dubai in 2014. Over the past decade, her Tashas hospitality group has grown to 14 outlets across the country, employing more than 1,000 people. But the US-Israel war with Iran is now taking a heavy toll on her business. Sideris says many of her restaurants, which are popular with both residents and expats, have seen revenues fall by more than 50%. But outlets that depend heavily on tourists have been hit much harder, with declines of 70% to 80%. The crisis has forced her to cut salaries by 30% for all staff including herself. "The current situation is brutal," she says. "I had a choice – either fire 30% of my staff or cut salaries to save jobs. I chose the latter for now." Sideris adds that the impact would have been worse if many of her outlets were not located inside community malls and close to residential neighbourhoods, where they still rely on local customers. The current tough reality is playing out across much of Dubai's restaurant sector. One senior executive at a restaurant chain, who asked not to be named, said footfall at its outlets has dropped to just 15-20% of normal, forcing them to place more than half of staff on unpaid leave. "We have no option," he says. "We've already shut down a few outlets temporarily, and the rest are operating with minimal staff." The impact is not limited to restaurants. The entire tourism ecosystem – from hotels and travel agencies, to transport companies and airlines – is feeling the strain. Over the past two decades, Dubai has built itself into one of the world's leading tourism hubs. Last year, the emirate welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally. But since the war began, that momentum has been sharply disrupted. The wider UAE has come under repeated attacks, with Dubai among the key targets of Iran's military response following US and Israeli strikes. Authorities say more than 2,400 missiles and drones have been launched towards the UAE, targeting airports, ports and civilian areas, including hotels and residential buildings. More than 90% of them were intercepted and destroyed, officials say. But some debris has fallen across parts of Dubai, including major residential areas, hotels and the airport. Images of fragments striking the Fairmont hotel on the upscale Palm Island were circulated widely online. To date, 11 people have been killed and more than 185 injured across the UAE, according to authorities in the country. The conflict, which began on 28 February, has disrupted air travel across the region. In the early weeks, tens of thousands of visitors were stranded before being evacuated on special flights. Thousands of regular, scheduled flights have been cancelled since the conflict began, bringing one of the region's busiest travel hubs to a halt at times. Dubai International Airport – the world's busiest for international passengers – handled 95.2 million travellers last year.  Some operations have since resumed, with flag-carrier Emirates operating a reduced flight schedule while working to restore full network operations. But with tourists leaving and the number of new arrivals collapsing, hotel stays in Dubai have fallen steeply. Occupancy levels across Dubai hotels dropped to between 15% and 20% of the usual level for this time of the year in the weeks following the outbreak of the war, according to Mamoun Hmiden, chief business officer at travel booking firm Wego. Hotels have responded with deep discounts, particularly during the Eid period, in an attempt to attract residents. Some luxury properties on Palm Jumeirah, one of the city's premium hotel hubs, have cut prices by as much as half. "The uncertainty is disrupting everyone at the moment," says Hmiden. Some hospitality chains have temporarily shut down some properties or closed certain sections, citing scheduled renovations – a move typically seen during the quieter summer months. A senior executive at an international hospitality group said occupancy at some properties had fallen to single digits. "It made sense to cut operational costs by shutting down for a few weeks and reviewing the situation later," he says. Even business hotels are under pressure. Dubai, a major hub for conferences and events, has seen organisers cancel or postpone large gatherings in the coming months. Majestic Hotels, which operates around 450 rooms across three properties, says occupancy has dropped to record lows. "We are seeing cancellations beyond April," says Varun Raj, cluster director of sales and marketing. "A lot of events have been cancelled, making it difficult for travellers to plan ahead." The slowdown comes after several years of rapid growth. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Dubai was among the first destinations to reopen to international visitors, allowing its tourism sector to recover faster than many global peers. Since then, it has expanded into a broader and more diversified market – strengthening its position as a luxury destination, while also attracting large numbers of mid-market and price-sensitive travellers from regions such as South Asia, Europe and the former Soviet states. That surge in demand has been matched by a sharp increase in supply. Years of growth have driven expansion not only in hotel capacity, but also in short-term apartment rentals across the city. That additional supply is now under pressure. Data firm AirDNA shared that a little over 226,500 short-term bookings were cancelled across the UAE between February 28 to March 29, the first month since the war began.   The downturn is also being felt by the migrant workforce that form the backbone of Dubai's hospitality industry – from restaurant staff to hotel workers.  As demand weakens, many have seen their hours reduced, or they have been placed on unpaid leave. While the UAE's labour system allows companies to adjust quickly to changing conditions, that flexibility can leave workers exposed to sudden income losses. "It feels like we are back to the Covid-19 period," says a South Asian waiter working at a high-end restaurant. There are fears we could lose our jobs again and be forced to go back home." He and several colleagues have been placed on unpaid leave, with no clarity on when – or if – they will return to work. Some hotels, including five-star properties, have started laying off employees. Rights groups say many migrant workers in the UAE are already financially vulnerable, with some carrying debt linked to recruitment fees. The impact of the war is also being felt across the wider Middle East. Research by Tourism Economics, part of Oxford Economics, suggests that between 23 million and 38 million fewer people could travel to the region this year, depending on how long the conflict continues. Between $34bn (£25bn) and $56bn in visitor spending could be lost. "If the war ends soon, there could be a quick recovery," says Hmiden. "But if it drags on, we have to start questioning the entire summer season." This week – Dubai announced $272.26 million in support for businesses, including tourism, over the next three to six months. Hotels will be allowed to delay sales-related fees and tourism dirham charges – a fee applied to guests staying in the city.  Authorities in Dubai are also working on plans to revive tourism once the conflict subsides, including new campaigns and promotional offers.  "The war is out of our control," says one official. "But we are preparing for when it ends." More like this: • How the Iran war is affecting global travel • How a prolonged Middle East conflict could reshape how we fly • Is Dubai's glossy image under threat? Sideris is hoping that landlords will provide rent relief in the form of deferred payments or reduced payments for the time being to support local businesses. For Sideris, the outlook remains uncertain. She says a recovery is possible from October if the war ends soon. But if the conflict continues, the timeline could shift to next year – bringing the risk of layoffs and outlet closures. "We've got enough cash to see us through a month or two... maximum three, and then past that, what do we do? After that, we will have to take tougher calls. Hopefully not. And this insanity ends soon." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . Business War News Features Iran war World of Business

##段落

2026年4月2日 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 Sameer Hashmi 去年迪拜接待了1959万名国际游客，使其成为全球到访量最大的城市之一，但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争对游客数量造成了毁灭性影响，当地企业正陷入困境。

##段落

在大多数夜晚，迪拜的餐厅通常座无虚席，食客和游客的持续喧嚣填满了城市各处的餐桌。但过去一个月，许多餐桌一直空着。对Natasha Sideris来说，这种转变来得突然而剧烈。她于2014年在迪拜开了第一家餐厅。过去十年间，她的Tashas餐饮集团已发展到全国14家门店，雇佣超过1000名员工。但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争现在正对她的生意造成沉重打击。

##段落

Sideris表示，她许多深受居民和外籍人士欢迎的餐厅收入下降了超过50%。但严重依赖游客的门店受到的冲击要大得多，降幅达70%至80%。这场危机迫使她将所有员工（包括她自己）的薪资削减30%。她说：“当前形势十分残酷。我面临一个选择——要么解雇30%的员工，要么降薪以保住工作。我暂时选择了后者。”

##段落

Sideris补充说，如果她的许多门店不是位于社区商场内、靠近居民区，仍然依赖本地客户，那么影响会更大。当前严峻的现实正在迪拜大部分餐饮行业上演。一家连锁餐厅的高级管理人员（要求匿名）表示，其门店客流量已降至正常水平的15%至20%，迫使他们让超过一半的员工无薪休假。“我们别无选择，”他说，“我们已经暂时关闭了几家门店，其余门店也以最低限度的人手运营。”

##段落

影响不仅限于餐厅。整个旅游生态系统——从酒店、旅行社到运输公司和航空公司——都感受到了压力。过去二十年间，迪拜已将自己打造成全球领先的旅游枢纽之一。去年，该酋长国接待了1959万名国际游客，使其成为全球到访量最大的城市之一。但自战争爆发以来，这一势头被急剧打断。

##段落

更广泛的阿联酋遭受了多次袭击，在美国和以色列发动打击后，迪拜是伊朗军事回应的主要目标之一。当局表示，超过2400枚导弹和无人机被射向阿联酋，目标是机场、港口和民用区域，包括酒店和住宅建筑。官员称其中超过90%被拦截并摧毁。但一些碎片已落在迪拜部分地区，包括

主要住宅区、酒店和机场。碎片击中高档棕榈岛上费尔蒙酒店的画面在网上广泛传播。据阿联酋当局称，截至目前，该国已有11人死亡，超过185人受伤。这场始于2月28日的冲突，已扰乱了整个地区的航空旅行。冲突初期，数万名游客被困，随后通过特别航班撤离。自冲突爆发以来，数千架次定期航班被取消，使该地区最繁忙的旅行枢纽之一时常陷入停滞。迪拜国际机场——全球国际旅客吞吐量最大的机场——去年接待了9520万名旅客。部分运营已恢复，旗舰航空公司阿联酋航空在努力恢复全面航线网络的同时，运营着缩减的航班计划。但随着游客离开和新抵达人数骤降，迪拜的酒店入住率大幅下滑。据旅行预订公司Wego的首席商务官马蒙·赫米登称，战争爆发后的数周内，迪拜各酒店的入住率降至往年同期正常水平的15%至20%。酒店纷纷推出大幅折扣，尤其是在开斋节期间，以吸引本地居民。朱美拉棕榈岛——该市高端酒店集中地之一——的一些豪华物业价格已削减近一半。“目前，不确定性正在扰乱每个人，”赫米登表示。一些酒店连锁集团以计划中的翻修为由，暂时关闭部分物业或部分区域——此举通常在较为冷清的夏季出现。一家国际酒店集团的高级高管表示，部分物业的入住率已降至个位数。“关闭几周以削减运营成本，之后再评估情况，是合理的做法，”他说。即使是商务酒店也面临压力。迪拜是会议和活动的主要枢纽，但组织者已取消或推迟未来数月的大型聚会。经营三家物业、共约450间客房的雄伟酒店集团表示，入住率已降至历史最低。“我们看到4月之后的取消订单，”该集团销售与市场集群总监瓦伦·拉杰说。“许多活动已被取消，让旅行者难以提前规划。”这一放缓发生在数年的快速增长之后。新冠疫情期间，迪拜是最早向国际游客重新开放的目的地之一，使其旅游业比许多全球同行恢复得更快。自那时起，它已扩展为一个更广泛、更多元化的市场——巩固了其作为奢华目的地的地位，同时

同时也吸引了来自南亚、欧洲和前苏联国家等地区的大量中端市场和价格敏感型旅行者。需求的激增伴随着供应的急剧增加。多年的增长不仅推动了酒店容量的扩张，也促进了该市短租公寓的发展。这一额外供应现在面临压力。数据公司AirDNA分享称，在2月28日至3月29日期间，即战争开始后的第一个月，阿联酋各地有超过22.65万笔短期预订被取消。这种低迷也影响到了构成迪拜酒店业支柱的移民劳动力——从餐厅员工到酒店工作人员。随着需求减弱，许多人工作时间减少，或被安排无薪休假。尽管阿联酋的劳动制度允许企业快速适应变化的条件，但这种灵活性可能使工人面临突然的收入损失。“感觉我们又回到了新冠时期，”一位在高端餐厅工作的南亚服务员说。“我们担心可能再次失业，被迫回国。”他和几位同事已被安排无薪休假，不清楚何时或是否能重返工作岗位。一些酒店，包括五星级酒店，已开始裁员。权利组织表示，阿联酋许多移民工人在经济上已经脆弱，一些人背负着与招聘费用相关的债务。战争的影响也波及整个中东地区。牛津经济研究院旗下旅游经济学公司的研究表明，根据冲突持续的时间长短，今年可能有2300万至3800万人减少前往该地区，游客支出可能损失340亿至560亿美元。“如果战争很快结束，可能会出现快速复苏，”Hmiden说。“但如果拖延下去，我们就不得不开始质疑整个夏季旺季。”本周，迪拜宣布在未来三到六个月内为包括旅游业在内的企业提供2.7226亿美元的支持。酒店将被允许推迟支付销售相关费用和旅游迪拉姆费用——这是对入住该市客人的收费。迪拜当局也在制定计划，一旦冲突平息，将重振旅游业，包括新的宣传活动和促销优惠。“战争超出了我们的控制，”一位官员说。“但我们正在为结束做准备。”更多类似内容：•伊朗战争如何影响全球旅行•中东长期冲突如何重塑我们的飞行方式•迪拜的光鲜形象是否受到威胁？Sideris希望房东能通过延期付款或暂时减少付款的形式提供租金减免，以支持当地企业。至于Si

deris，前景仍不确定。她表示，如果战争能尽快结束，从十月开始可能复苏。但若冲突持续，时间表可能推迟至明年——这将带来裁员和门店关闭的风险。“我们的现金足以支撑一两个月……最多三个月，之后我们该怎么办？届时，我们将不得不做出更艰难的决定。希望不会如此，希望这场疯狂尽快结束。”——如需面向董事会及更广泛领域的全球洞察与专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》通讯，而《基本清单》则提供精选特写与见解。欲获取更多商业及更广泛资讯，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业 战争 新闻 特写 伊朗战争 《商业世界》

readings.title: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
body: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
What separates the very best in the world from the remaining 7 billion of us?

Exceptional talent often looks like an act of revolution — a person doing something in a way no one has ever done it before — but many revolutionary talents are actually built on a foundation of evolutionary tweaks. These tweaks develop over time, often compensating for weaknesses and anxieties that might derail a lesser talent.
For all his brilliance, though, Messi is famously anxious. For several years, he habitually vomited on the field before big matches.

Take the world’s best soccer player, an Argentinean named Lionel Messi. Messi has won more Ballon d’Or trophies, awarded to the best soccer player of the year, than any other player. He has scored more goals in a calendar year than any other living player, is the top all-time scorer in Spain’s La Liga, and has the highest goal ratio in the sport today, scoring almost once every match.

For all his brilliance, though, he’s famously anxious. For several years, Messi habitually vomited on the field before big matches. After a string of disappointing national-team losses, another former Argentinean giant of the game, the late Diego Maradona, uncharitably criticized Messi by suggesting that it was “useless trying to make a leader out of a man who goes to the toilet twenty times before a game.”

Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, and many of the world’s best grapple with anxiety precisely because they expect so much from themselves. But Messi hasn’t allowed his anxiety to diminish his brilliance because he’s mastered a coping mechanism that also doubles as the secret behind his tactical brilliance.
Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Second, he scopes out the opposition.

A soccer match runs for 90 minutes (plus a few minutes for “injury time”), and most players are active in the game from the first minute. As soon as the whistle blows, they implore their teammates to pass the ball and pursue the tactics their coaches laid out before the game.

But Messi is famous for not playing the game during its opening minutes. This is his evolutionary tweak, which developed as he played the game at progressively higher levels. For the opening minutes, Messi ambles back and forth near the middle of the field and almost never engages with his teammates. Whereas other players run and sometimes sprint, Messi spends much of his time walking, rarely breaking into more than a slow jog.

Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Easing into the game is Messi’s way of ensuring he’s fully engaged for the remainder of the game. His on-field vomiting has resolved itself, in part perhaps because he’s found a more effective way to calm his nerves. Second, he spends this time scoping out the opposition. His legs move slowly, but his eyes dart from player to player, assessing his opponents’ strengths, weaknesses, and tactics, and monitoring his own team’s movement with and around the ball. Messi is less valuable to his team early in the game, but this tactical pause elevates his value for the remaining 95 percent of the game.

If you split soccer game play into “preparatory” and “engaged” components, Messi leans heavily on preparation. During one classic game between Messi’s Barcelona and archrivals Real Madrid, in 2017, Messi ran for just four minutes and walked for more than eighty of the game’s ninety minutes. When he was engaged, though, he was dynamic, creating nine chances, scoring one goal, and feeding the ball to a teammate who scored another goal.
As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act.

That pattern isn’t unusual for Messi, and it’s often in the biggest games that he accentuates his in-game preparation. That preparation also explains his ability to find himself in the right place at the right time, over and over. Though his positional play appears otherworldly, it isn’t a miracle; it’s that he’s learned, minute by minute, that a particular defender leaves a particular square of pitch uncovered or that two midfielders leave a small corner of the pitch open when they gravitate to the middle of the field.
The lesson for the rest of us is clear: When you’re anxious, whether in athletics or in life more broadly, pause. Slow down . Prepare.

As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act. Judson Brewer, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist, has spent much of his career thinking about how to do nothing.
About fifteen years ago, Brewer developed a mindfulness-based treatment for addiction.
His approach instructs addicts to resist the waves of anxiety during moments of craving by following the four steps of an approach that goes by the acronym RAIN:
I nvestigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., “What is happening in my body now?”)
N ote what is happening from moment to moment.

Brewer has said that his approach was inspired by clinical psychologist Tara Brach’s . To test the approach, Brewer worked with smokers who were struggling to quit. Nicotine addiction is notoriously stubborn — more so than many harder drugs that produce stronger immediate responses in users.

Before unleashing the program on smokers, Brewer wanted to test the system on himself. The problem was “I was a nonsmoker,” Brewer wrote, “who needed to be able to relate to patients who felt as though their heads were going to explode unless they smoked.”

Nicotine has a half-life of around two hours, so to begin, smokers need to resist the urge to light up for two hours at a time. Brewer reasoned that smokers who could last two hours without a cigarette would cultivate new nonsmoking habits, extending those stretches till they no longer felt the urge to smoke at all.

He simulated these periods of resistance by learning to meditate for two-hour stretches without moving. During moments of restlessness, he followed the RAIN steps — recognize, allow, investigate, note — and if he moved his body, the clock would reset, and he’d have to start again.

This might sound easy, but two hours is a long time to sit still without entertainment. “Surprisingly it wasn’t the physical pain of not shifting for a long time that got me,” Brewer wrote. “It was the restlessness … Those cravings shouted, ‘Get up!’ ”
Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean.

For many months, Brewer would get close, then restlessness would defeat him. “Then one day,” he wrote, “I did it. I sat for the full two hours … Each subsequent sit got easier and easier because I had the confidence that it could be done. And I knew that my patients could quit smoking. They simply needed the proper tools.”

Brewer was right. His patients had been stuck, incapable of quitting one of the most addictive substances on earth. But when he ran study after study, pitting his RAIN mindfulness method against the most effective addiction treatment approaches of the day, his approach was more than twice as effective.

Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean. They were more than five times as likely to have shaken their addictions using an approach that essentially taught them to pause at the moment their bodies were most urgently driving them to act.

Of the four steps in Brewer’s RAIN approach, the second — allowing — is perhaps the most critical. Allowing an experience to wash over you sounds disarmingly easy because it doesn’t require you to do anything. But that’s exactly the point. It’s difficult because you’re forced to do nothing despite the urge to act.

是什么将世界顶尖高手与其余70亿人区分开来？

非凡的才华往往看起来像一场革命——一个人以从未有人尝试过的方式做事——但许多革命性的才华实际上建立在渐进式微调的基石之上。这些微调随时间发展，常常弥补那些可能击垮普通人才的弱点与焦虑。

然而，尽管梅西才华横溢，他却以焦虑闻名。多年来，他在重大比赛前习惯性地在球场上呕吐。

以世界最佳足球运动员、阿根廷人莱昂内尔·梅西为例。梅西赢得金球奖（颁发给年度最佳足球运动员的奖项）的次数超过任何其他球员。他在一个日历年内的进球数超过任何其他现役球员，是西班牙西甲联赛的历史最佳射手，并且拥有当今足坛最高的进球率，几乎每场比赛都能进球。

然而，尽管他光芒四射，他却以焦虑著称。多年来，梅西习惯性地在重大比赛前于球场上呕吐。在一连串令人失望的国家队失利之后，另一位已故的阿根廷足球巨擘迭戈·马拉多纳毫不客气地批评梅西，暗示“试图把一个赛前上厕所二十次的人培养成领袖是徒劳的”。

拥有惊人的天赋并不能让你对焦虑免疫，而世界上许多顶尖选手恰恰因为对自己期望过高而深陷焦虑。但梅西没有让焦虑削弱他的光芒，因为他掌握了一种应对机制，这种机制同时也正是他战术智慧背后的秘密。

梅西在开场几分钟内做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。第二，他观察对手。

一场足球比赛持续90分钟（外加几分钟“伤停补时”），大多数球员从第一分钟起就投入比赛。哨声一响，他们便恳求队友传球，并执行教练赛前布置的战术。

但梅西以在开场几分钟不参与比赛而闻名。这是他的渐进式微调，是他在越来越高的比赛水平中逐渐发展出来的。在开场几分钟里，梅西在中场附近来回踱步，几乎不与队友互动。当其他球员奔跑甚至冲刺时，梅西大部分时间在行走，很少超过慢跑的速度。

梅西在这最初的几分钟里做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。慢慢进入比赛状态是梅

ssi确保自己在比赛剩余时间内全神贯注的方式。他在场上呕吐的问题已经自行解决，部分原因可能是他找到了更有效的平复神经的方法。其次，他会利用这段时间观察对手。他的双腿移动缓慢，但目光却从一名球员扫向另一名球员，评估对手的优势、劣势和战术，同时留意自己球队在有球和无球时的跑动。梅西在比赛初期对球队的价值较低，但这种战术性的停顿提升了他在比赛剩余95%时间里的价值。

如果你将足球比赛分为“准备”和“投入”两个部分，梅西非常依赖准备。在2017年梅西所在的巴塞罗那对阵宿敌皇家马德里的一场经典比赛中，梅西在90分钟的比赛里只跑了四分钟，走了八十多分钟。然而，当他投入时，他充满活力，创造了九次机会，打入一球，并助攻队友再进一球。

正如你可能想象的那样，停顿比听起来要难得多。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。

这种模式对梅西来说并不罕见，而且往往在最重大的比赛中，他会更加突出赛前准备。这种准备也解释了他为什么能一次又一次地在正确的时间出现在正确的位置。尽管他的位置感看起来超凡脱俗，但这并非奇迹；而是他每分钟都在学习，比如某位特定后卫会漏掉球场某个区域，或者两名中场球员向中路靠拢时会留下球场的一小块空当。

对我们其他人的启示很明确：当你感到焦虑时，无论是在体育竞技还是更广泛的生活中，要停顿下来。放慢节奏。做好准备。

正如你可能想象的那样，停顿比听起来要难得多。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。贾德森·布鲁尔，一位精神病学家和神经科学家，职业生涯的大部分时间都在思考如何“什么都不做”。

大约十五年前，布鲁尔开发了一种基于正念的成瘾治疗方法。

他的方法指导成瘾者在渴望发作时，通过遵循一个缩写为RAIN的四步法来抵抗焦虑浪潮：

R——识别正在升起的情绪。

A——允许它存在。

I——探究你的情绪和想法（例如，“我身体里现在发生了什么？”）。

N——注意每一刻正在发生的事情。

布鲁尔曾表示，他的方法受到临床心理学家塔拉·布拉赫的启发。为了测试这种方法，布鲁尔与努力戒烟的吸烟者合作。尼古丁成瘾以顽固著称——比许多能产生更强即时反应的硬性毒品更难戒除。

在推出该计划之前

在吸烟者身上，布鲁尔想在自己身上测试这个系统。问题是，“我是个不吸烟者，”布鲁尔写道，“却需要能与那些觉得不抽烟头就要爆炸的患者产生共鸣。”  
尼古丁的半衰期大约为两小时，因此起初，吸烟者需要每次抵抗住两小时不点烟的冲动。布鲁尔推断，能坚持两小时不吸烟的吸烟者会培养出新的不吸烟习惯，逐步延长这些时段，直到他们完全不再感到吸烟的冲动。  
他通过练习静坐冥想两小时不动来模拟这些抵抗期。在烦躁不安的时刻，他遵循RAIN步骤——识别、允许、探究、注意——如果他移动了身体，时钟就会重置，他得重新开始。  
这可能听起来容易，但静坐两小时不动且无娱乐是漫长的。“令人惊讶的是，长时间不动带来的身体疼痛并没有难住我，”布鲁尔写道。“而是烦躁……那些渴望在呐喊：‘起来！’”  
几个月后，当其他治疗方案的大多数患者复发时，他的正念小组保持洁净。  
数月来，布鲁尔常接近目标，然后烦躁击败了他。“然后有一天，”他写道，“我做到了。我坐满了整整两小时……每次后续静坐都越来越容易，因为我有信心能完成。我知道我的患者能戒烟。他们只需要合适的工具。”  
布鲁尔是对的。他的患者曾陷入困境，无法戒除地球上最易上瘾的物质之一。但当他进行一项又一项研究，将他的RAIN正念方法与当时最有效的成瘾治疗方法对比时，他的方法效果是它们的两倍多。  
几个月后，当其他治疗方案的大多数患者复发时，他的正念小组保持洁净。他们摆脱成瘾的可能性高出五倍多，这种方法本质上是教他们在身体最迫切驱使他们行动的时刻暂停。  
在布鲁尔RAIN方法的四个步骤中，第二步——允许——或许最为关键。允许一种体验冲刷过你，听起来出奇地简单，因为它不要求你做任何事。但这正是重点。它之所以困难，是因为尽管有行动的冲动，你却被迫无所作为。  
尽管暂停和准备益处多多，但有时主事件并不按计划进行。梅西输过无数场比赛，而布鲁尔的尼古丁成瘾者并非都在实验结束后数周或数月保持戒断。掌握这些失败后伴随的焦虑和不适至关重要，而这是其中一项关键技能。

取得突破的人与长期陷入困境的人之间的主要区别。

readings.title: Why “Lake America” isn’t funny
body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff Why “Lake America” isn’t funny ﻿Trump’s lake stunt, briefly explained. by Cameron Peters Aug 27, 2026, 10:20 PM UTC Gift Donald Trump displays a map labeling Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in the Oval Office of the White House on August 27, 2026. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump says he’s renaming Lake Ontario. Let’s talk about it. Can he really do that? Probably, though it doesn’t mean anyone will listen. Strictly speaking, Trump’s executive order, signed Thursday in the Oval Office, directs the Interior Department to update the lake’s name to “Lake America” in the US’s Geographic Names Information System. It remains to be seen whether products like Apple and Google maps will follow suit, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, whose state contains the US portion of the lake, says she won’t . Why is he doing that? The immediate answer is that Trump launched a trade war with Canada over the weekend, and he’s mad that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney won’t give him what he wants; this is a petty way to lash out. That doesn’t explain the trade war itself, though. Unfortunately, when my colleague, noted Canadian resident Zack Beauchamp, went looking earlier this week, he couldn’t find an explanation either. As he writes , there’s absolutely no constituency for this fight — other than Trump’s own imperial desires as he keeps joking-but-maybe-not-joking about making Canada the 51st state. The view from a very angry Canada Isn’t this just a stupid stunt? It’s a stupid stunt — but not just that. As my colleague Caitlin Dewey wrote earlier this week and Zack can attest, Canadians are royally pissed at the US. The trade war might feel like one more Trump fit of pique to Americans, but for Canadians, it’s a serious threat. Thursday’s executive order further ratchets up those tensions, and it specifically plays into the (very credible) school of thought that Trump isn’t really in this to redress US-Canada trade imbalances; as with many things Trump, it’s about dominance and the desire to claim a “win” at any cost. Lastly, it’s worth dwelling for a second on the stunt itself. One, Lake Ontario isn’t Canada’s name for it; it predates either country. And two, ad hoc renaming of bodies of water — this isn’t even the first time this Trump term — puts Trump in some fairly uncomfortable company . My colleague Sara Herschander just debuted her new newsletter, Nice Things, which feels like a great fit for this section. It’s all about dreaming big to build a better America, one with widespread high-speed rail, affordable housing, and infrastructure that works. You can subscribe here and read a story from the first edition here . Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow! ##段落
政治 / 唐纳德·特朗普 / 《The Logoff》 为什么“美洲湖”并不好笑 特朗普的湖泊噱头，简要解释。作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯 2026年8月27日，晚上10:20 UTC 赠送 唐纳德·特朗普于2026年8月27日在白宫椭圆形办公室展示一张将安大略湖标注为“美洲湖”的地图。安德鲁·哈尼克/盖蒂图片社 卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的编辑。本文首发于《The Logoff》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你了解特朗普政府动态，同时不让政治新闻占据你的生活。在此订阅。

##段落
欢迎来到《The Logoff》：唐纳德·特朗普说他要把安大略湖改名。让我们来聊聊这件事。他真的能这么做吗？可能可以，但这不意味着会有人听。严格来说，特朗普周四在椭圆形办公室签署的行政命令，指示内政部在美国地理名称信息系统中将该湖的名称更新为“美洲湖”。苹果和谷歌地图等产品是否会跟进还有待观察，但纽约州州长凯西·霍楚尔——该州拥有该湖的美国部分——表示她不会配合。他为什么要这么做？直接的回答是，特朗普在周末对加拿大发动了贸易战，而他恼火于加拿大总理马克·卡尼不给他想要的东西；这是一种小气的发泄方式。但这并不能解释贸易战本身。不幸的是，当我的同事、知名加拿大居民扎克·博尚本周早些时候去寻找答案时，他也找不到解释。正如他所写的，这场斗争完全没有支持者——除了特朗普自己不断开玩笑但可能并非玩笑的、想让加拿大成为第51个州的帝国野心。

##段落
从一个非常愤怒的加拿大的视角来看 这不只是一个愚蠢的噱头吗？这是一个愚蠢的噱头——但不仅仅是。正如我的同事凯特琳·杜威本周早些时候所写、扎克也能证实的，加拿大人对美国极为愤怒。贸易战在美国人看来可能只是特朗普又一次意气用事，但对加拿大人来说，这是一个严重的威胁。周四的行政命令进一步加剧了这些紧张局势，并且特别印证了一种（非常可信的）观点，即特朗普的真正目的并非纠正美加贸易失衡；正如特朗普的许多事情一样，这关乎霸权和不惜一切代价“取胜”的欲望。最后，值得花点时间审视一下这个噱头本身。第一，安大略湖并不是加拿大起的名字；它比这两个国家的历史都更悠久。第二，随意给水域改名——这甚至不是特朗普本届任期内第一次这么做了——让特朗普置身于一些相当令人不安的同侪之列。

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.

有效领导的3个策略，来自一位前宇航员
2023年12月4日
/
约瑟夫·德布林
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
Reddit
WhatsApp
玛丽亚·彼得里希娜 / iStock
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> 玛丽亚·彼得里希娜 / iStock
领导力是什么样的？

虽然带领团队的方法多种多样，但许多人在寻找有效领导风格时，都会遇到一些共同的问题：我该如何支持我的团队？我需要命令别人尊重，还是赢得尊重？而最关键的问题是：我怎样才能确保团队信任我？

凯迪·科尔曼在作为化学家、工程师、空军上校和宇航员的职业生涯中，一直在面对这些问题。在与TED科学策展人大卫·比埃洛的对话中，科尔曼分享了建立并维持领导者信任的三种策略。无论你的职业是什么，这些建议都能帮助你让团队准备好迎接你遇到的任何挑战——无论是在外太空还是在地球上。

人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有。

1. 勇敢地去了解你的团队成员，把他们当作独立的个体

人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有，科尔曼说。你团队中的每个成员都是一个完整的人，而由于我们在工作中遇到的许多问题都是跨学科的，了解每个人在朝九晚五之外是什么样的，是非常有价值的。以足够的坦诚，用这种方式去了解你的团队，是任何领导者必备的技能。

科尔曼说，当你能说出“我觉得你的世界和我的不同，我想更多地了解它”时，你不仅仅是在建立信任；你是在打开一条沟通渠道，让你更了解队友的特质。这种对话需要愿意和勇气去展现脆弱。一旦你知道每个人能带来什么，你就能培养那些能带领团队走向集体成功的特质。

例如，当科尔曼为空间站生活做准备时，她的顾问警告说，长时间离开家人可能难以承受。然而，对她来说，这不是问题——她已经通勤并远离家人工作十多年了。在分享了自己的经历后，她的同事意识到，她不仅能适应空间站的生活，还能帮助其他人应对这种变化。

2. 创造一种对每个人的想法都开放的文化

虽然领导者必须引导团队，但同样重要的是，让每个人都知道他们可以为自己发声，并把自己的想法带到台面上来。

科尔曼在NASA训练时，就受益于这样的领导力，当时她正在为前往太空做准备。

面对预算削减，美国国家航空航天局宣布将淘汰较小号的太空服，这意味着如果某人不符合使用较大号太空服的资格，就无法前往空间站。这对科尔曼来说是一个选择：等待NASA获得适合她的太空服，或者想办法训练自己使用较大的太空服。通过与NASA的决策者合作，科尔曼得以调整训练，使用较大的太空服。她说，如果她没有感到可以自由发声，她可能会等上十年才能穿着小号太空服前往空间站。  
当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。  
##段落
3. 让信任成为你的使命  
有时在工作场所建立信任可能比你预期的更困难，但当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。职场动态总是在变化——也许队友的工作/生活优先级发生了转变，或者一个大错误要求你们在新压力下共同合作。这些挑战使培养信任变得棘手，但它们也是机遇的时刻。  
如果出现了新的挑战或信任被破坏，科尔曼提醒我们要“始终弄清楚原因和内容”。务必询问：为什么会发生这种情况，他们为什么会有这样的感受，以及可以对此做些什么？对不同观点保持开放态度，如果一开始没有突破，不要放弃。联系往往体现在你做的那些小事中：谈论食物或音乐，写一张便条赞美一个想法并请求了解更多。这种联系和脆弱的程度起初可能看起来不太直观，但当你把信任作为使命的核心部分时，它就会变得容易。  
科尔曼提醒我们，信任既是给予的，也是赢得的。作为一名女性，她知道赢得一些男性同事的信任可能格外具有挑战性。她的方法很简单：她表现出色，并以耐心和坚持，学会了同事们的语言，也教会了他们她的语言。建立信任的挑战将永远存在，但如果你为团队树立脆弱、开放和理解的榜样，你会发现回报也永远存在。  
这篇文章改编自最近一次与凯迪·科尔曼的LinkedIn Live对话，她是前NASA宇航员，即将出版的新书《共享空间：宇航员的任务、奇迹与变革指南》将于2024年7月发行。  
在这里观看完整的LinkedIn对话：  
来自我们合作伙伴美国空军的消息：美国空军的使命是飞行、战斗并获胜——随时随地提供空中力量。无论是全职、兼职、穿制服还是不穿制服，每个服役人员都在帮助我们实现任务成功中扮演着关键角色。

dialogs.title: At the check-in counter
dialogs.goal: 练习护照/行李/座位相关表达，从容应对值机

lines.en: Good morning. May I see your passport and booking reference, please?
lines.zh: 早上好，请出示您的护照和预订编号。

lines.en: Sure, here you are. I'd like a window seat if possible.
lines.zh: 好的，给您。如果可以的话我想要靠窗的座位。

lines.en: I can arrange that. Are you checking in any bags today?
lines.zh: 可以安排。您今天有要托运的行李吗？

lines.en: Just one suitcase. Does it meet the weight limit?
lines.zh: 就一个行李箱。它超重了吗？

lines.en: It's within the limit. Your boarding pass is ready — gate 22, boarding at 10:40.
lines.zh: 在限额内。您的登机牌好了——22 号登机口，10:40 登机。

lines.en: Great. Could you also confirm that my carry-on bag fits the cabin size requirements?
lines.zh: 太好了。您能再确认一下我的随身行李符合客舱尺寸要求吗？

lines.en: Let me check the dimensions. Yes, it fits within our standard allowance. You're all set for the cabin.
lines.zh: 让我看一下尺寸。是的，符合我们的标准限额。您的客舱行李没问题。

lines.en: Perfect. By the way, is there any chance I could get an aisle seat instead? I just realized I may need to stretch my legs.
lines.zh: 太好了。顺便问一下，我能改成过道座位吗？我刚意识到可能需要伸伸腿。

lines.en: Certainly. Let me update that for you — I've moved you to 21C, an aisle seat. No problem at all.
lines.zh: 当然可以。我来为您更新——已为您调到21C，过道座位。完全没问题。

lines.en: Thank you so much. One last thing — what time should I be at the gate?
lines.zh: 非常感谢。最后问一下，我应该在什么时间到登机口？

lines.en: Please be at the gate at least 30 minutes before boarding. Enjoy your flight, and have a wonderful trip!
lines.zh: 请在登机前至少30分钟到达登机口。祝您飞行愉快，旅途顺利！

dialogs.title: Small talk at a conference
dialogs.goal: 用自然的破冰句开启商务对话，并过渡到合作话题

lines.en: Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm Echo, from the consumer insights team.
lines.zh: 你好，我们好像还没见过。我是 Echo，来自消费者洞察团队。

lines.en: Nice to meet you. I work on product strategy. What brings you to this session?
lines.zh: 很高兴认识你。我做产品策略。你为什么来听这场？

lines.en: I'm exploring how AI is changing our research methods. Have you seen anything useful today?
lines.zh: 我在研究 AI 如何改变我们的研究方法。你今天有看到什么有用的吗？

lines.en: Actually, yes — a talk on real-time consumer signals. We should compare notes sometime.
lines.zh: 其实有——一个关于实时消费者信号的演讲。我们应该找个时间交流一下。

lines.en: I'd love that. Let's grab coffee after the keynote.
lines.zh: 太好了。主题演讲后我们喝杯咖啡吧。

lines.en: Sounds good. By the way, how does your team currently handle qualitative data?
lines.zh: 听起来不错。顺便问一下，你们团队目前是怎么处理定性数据的？

lines.en: We still rely heavily on manual coding, which is time-consuming. That's why I'm keen on AI-driven tools.
lines.zh: 我们还是主要靠人工编码，很耗时。所以我对 AI 驱动的工具很感兴趣。

lines.en: Interesting. We've been piloting a sentiment analysis model that might complement your workflow.
lines.zh: 有意思。我们一直在试点一个情绪分析模型，可能和你们的工作流互补。

lines.en: That sounds promising. Could you share a bit more about how it handles multilingual data?
lines.zh: 听起来很有前景。你能多分享一下它如何处理多语言数据吗？

lines.en: Sure — it's trained on several major languages, but accuracy varies. Maybe we can set up a quick demo next week.
lines.zh: 当然——它在几种主要语言上训练过，但准确率有差异。也许我们下周可以安排一个快速演示。

lines.en: Perfect. I'll bring our research lead along. Let's exchange contacts and follow up by email.
lines.zh: 完美。我会带上我们的研究负责人。我们交换一下联系方式，然后邮件跟进吧。

dialogs.title: Checking into a hotel
dialogs.goal: 掌握入住登记、特殊需求与Wi-Fi等常用句

lines.en: Good evening. Do you have a reservation under the name Lee?
lines.zh: 晚上好。请问有预订在 Lee 名下吗？

lines.en: Yes, for two nights. Is breakfast included?
lines.zh: 有的，住两晚。含早餐吗？

lines.en: It is — served from 7 to 10. Could I have a room on a higher floor, away from the elevator?
lines.zh: 含的——7 点到 10 点供应。可以安排高一点、远离电梯的房间吗？

lines.en: Certainly. Here's your key card, and the Wi-Fi password is on this slip.
lines.zh: 当然可以。这是您的房卡，Wi-Fi 密码在这张纸上。

lines.en: Thank you. Could you also confirm the checkout time for me?
lines.zh: 谢谢。另外能帮我确认一下退房时间吗？

lines.en: Checkout is at noon, but we offer a late checkout until 2 PM for an additional fee.
lines.zh: 退房时间是中午12点，不过我们可以提供延迟至下午2点的退房服务，需额外收费。

lines.en: That's good to know. I might take advantage of that. Is there a gym or pool on site?
lines.zh: 这信息很有用，我可能会用到。酒店内有健身房或游泳池吗？

lines.en: Yes, both are on the second floor, open from 6 AM to 10 PM. Towels are provided at the front desk.
lines.zh: 有的，两者都在二楼，开放时间为早上6点到晚上10点。毛巾可在前台领取。

lines.en: Perfect. One more thing — could you arrange a wake-up call at 7:30 tomorrow morning?
lines.zh: 太好了。还有一件事——能帮我安排明早7:30的叫醒服务吗？

lines.en: Of course. I've noted that for room 1208. Is there anything else you need?
lines.zh: 当然可以。我已为您记录在1208房间。还有其他需要吗？

lines.en: No, that's all for now. Thanks for your help.
lines.zh: 暂时没有了，谢谢你的帮助。

dialogs.title: Ordering with dietary needs
dialogs.goal: 清晰表达过敏/忌口，避免误会

lines.en: Welcome! Have you decided what you'd like to order?
lines.zh: 欢迎！您决定好点什么了吗？

lines.en: Not yet. I'm allergic to peanuts — could you tell me which dishes are safe?
lines.zh: 还没。我对花生过敏——能告诉我哪些菜是安全的吗？

lines.en: Of course. The grilled fish and the vegetable soup are both nut-free. I'll note the allergy for the kitchen.
lines.zh: 当然。烤鱼和蔬菜汤都不含坚果。我会在厨房单上标注过敏。

lines.en: Perfect, thank you. Could I also get that without spicy sauce?
lines.zh: 太好了，谢谢。那份可以不放辣酱吗？

lines.en: Absolutely. I'll make sure the chef prepares it with a mild seasoning instead. Would you like any appetizer to start?
lines.zh: 完全可以。我会确保厨师改用清淡调味。需要先来点开胃菜吗？

lines.en: Yes, the spring rolls look good — but are they fried in peanut oil?
lines.zh: 好的，春卷看起来不错——但那是用花生油炸的吗？

lines.en: Good question. We use canola oil for frying, so they're safe. However, the dipping sauce contains sesame paste — would you like it on the side?
lines.zh: 问得好。我们用菜籽油炸，所以是安全的。不过蘸酱含芝麻酱——需要单独放旁边吗？

lines.en: That would be great. Please keep the sauce separate, and I'll decide whether to use it.
lines.zh: 那太好了。请把酱单独放，我自己决定要不要用。

lines.en: Understood. I'll also check with the kitchen on the dessert options — the mango pudding is peanut-free, but the chocolate cake may contain traces.
lines.zh: 明白了。我还会和厨房确认甜点选项——芒果布丁不含花生，但巧克力蛋糕可能含微量。

lines.en: Thanks for being so thorough. I'll go with the mango pudding then.
lines.zh: 谢谢你这么仔细。那我就选芒果布丁吧。

lines.en: Great choice. I'll place your order now and confirm everything with the chef. Your safety is our priority.
lines.zh: 好选择。我现在下单并和厨师确认所有细节。您的安全是我们的首要任务。

dialogs.title: Talking about AI at work
dialogs.goal: 用职场商务英语表达对 AI 的看法与担忧

lines.en: Have you tried the new AI assistant? It's been a game-changer for my drafts.
lines.zh: 你试过新的 AI 助手了吗？它彻底改变了我写草稿的方式。

lines.en: I have, but I'm cautious. I double-check everything it produces.
lines.zh: 试过，但我比较谨慎。它生成的东西我都会复核。

lines.en: Fair enough. I see it as a starting point, not the final answer.
lines.zh: 有道理。我把它当作起点，而不是最终答案。

lines.en: Exactly. The human touch still matters most with our clients.
lines.zh: 没错。对咱们的客户来说，人情味依然最重要。

lines.en: That said, I've noticed it saves me at least two hours a day on research and summarization.
lines.zh: 话虽如此，我注意到它每天至少帮我在研究和总结上省下两个小时。

lines.en: I can see that. But what about accuracy? I've caught it making subtle errors in data interpretation.
lines.zh: 这我能理解。但准确性呢？我抓到过它在数据解读上犯一些很细微的错误。

lines.en: I've seen that too. That's why I always cross-reference its output with our internal reports.
lines.zh: 我也遇到过。所以我才总是拿它生成的内容和咱们内部报告做交叉核对。

lines.en: Good practice. My concern is more about long-term dependency—are we losing our own analytical skills?
lines.zh: 好习惯。我更担心的是长期依赖——我们会不会失去自己的分析能力？

lines.en: That's a valid point. I try to use it as a tool, not a crutch. I still do the critical thinking myself.
lines.zh: 这点提得很对。我尽量把它当工具，而不是拐杖。关键思考还是我自己来。

lines.en: I think we need a team guideline on when and how to use AI, especially for client-facing documents.
lines.zh: 我觉得咱们需要一份团队指南，明确什么时候、怎么用 AI，尤其是面对客户的文档。

lines.en: Agreed. Let's bring that up in next week's meeting—maybe we can draft a policy together.
lines.zh: 同意。咱们下周会上提一下——也许可以一起起草一份规范。

dialogs.title: Briefing a Descriptive Panel
dialogs.zhTitle: 为描述性感官评价小组做导入简报
dialogs.goal: 掌握主持感官评价小组时的标准指令语言与"去引导化"表达。

lines.en: Good morning, everyone. Before we start, a quick reminder: we are not looking for whether you like the sample. We are looking for what you perceive.
lines.zh: 早上好。开始之前提醒一下：我们不是要知道你喜不喜欢这个样品，而是要知道你感知到了什么。

lines.en: So we should keep preference out of it entirely?
lines.zh: 所以我们要完全把偏好排除在外？

lines.en: Exactly. Intensity, not preference. If something is very sweet and you personally hate it, the score is still high.
lines.zh: 正是。评的是强度，不是喜好。如果某样东西很甜而你个人讨厌它，分数依然要打高。

lines.en: Understood. And the order of the samples?
lines.zh: 明白了。样品顺序呢？

lines.en: Balanced and randomised, as always. Please cleanse your palate with water and the unsalted cracker between each one, and wait ninety seconds.
lines.zh: 照例是平衡随机化的。每个样品之间请用清水和无盐饼干清口，并等待 90 秒。

lines.en: What if I pick up an attribute that is not on the ballot?
lines.zh: 如果我感知到一个评分表上没有的属性怎么办？

lines.en: Write it in the open field. Honestly, those are often the most useful lines on the whole sheet.
lines.zh: 写在开放栏里。说实话，那些往往是整张表上最有价值的内容。

lines.en: Should I try to match the vocabulary we agreed on in training?
lines.zh: 我需要尽量用我们培训时统一的词汇吗？

lines.en: Use the lexicon where it fits, but do not force it. A forced term hides more than it reveals.
lines.zh: 合适的地方就用词典里的术语，但别硬套。硬套的术语掩盖的比揭示的多。

lines.en: One last thing — no discussion during evaluation. We compare notes only in the debrief.
lines.zh: 最后一点——评价过程中不要交流。我们只在总结环节比对结果。

keys.zh: 评强度，不评偏好（感官分析第一原则）
平衡随机化（样品呈送设计）

dialogs.title: Presenting Findings the Client Did Not Want
dialogs.zhTitle: 汇报一个客户不想听到的结论
dialogs.goal: 练习在坏消息中保持专业与建设性的商务表达。

lines.en: So, bottom line — does the new formulation win?
lines.zh: 所以，直接说结论——新配方赢了吗？

lines.en: Not on the measure you asked about. But I would argue you were asking about the wrong measure.
lines.zh: 在你问的那个指标上没有。但我认为，你问的可能不是该问的那个指标。

lines.en: Go on.
lines.zh: 你说。

lines.en: Overall liking is flat — statistically indistinguishable. However, the new formulation scores significantly higher on perceived care and product quality cues.
lines.zh: 总体喜好度持平，统计上无差异。但新配方在"感知到的用心程度"和"品质线索"上显著更高。

lines.en: Does that translate into anything commercial?
lines.zh: 这能转化成商业结果吗？

lines.en: It correlates strongly with repurchase intent in this category. Liking predicts the first purchase; quality cues predict the fourth.
lines.zh: 在这个品类里，它与复购意向高度相关。喜好度预测第一次购买，品质线索预测第四次。

lines.en: That is a bolder claim than I expected from you.
lines.zh: 这比我预期的你会说的话要大胆。

lines.en: It is in the appendix with the regression. I would rather show you the uncomfortable version now than the comfortable one in six months.
lines.zh: 附录里有回归结果。我宁愿现在给你看那个不舒服的版本，也不想六个月后给你看那个舒服的版本。

lines.en: Fair. What would you do if this were your decision?
lines.zh: 有道理。如果是你来定，你会怎么做？

lines.en: Ship it, but rewrite the claim. You are selling reassurance, not novelty.
lines.zh: 上市，但改掉宣称。你卖的是安心感，不是新奇感。

dialogs.title: A Tight Connection
dialogs.goal: 掌握机场改签、行李与登机口相关的高频表达。

lines.en: Excuse me, my inbound flight was delayed and I have fifty minutes to make my connection. Will I be all right?
lines.zh: 打扰一下，我来程航班延误了，中转只剩 50 分钟。来得及吗？

lines.en: It is tight but doable. Are you checked through to your final destination?
lines.zh: 有点紧但可以。您的行李是直挂到终点的吗？

lines.en: Yes, my luggage is tagged all the way through. Do I need to clear security again?
lines.zh: 是的，行李直挂到底。我需要重新过安检吗？

lines.en: You will, at the transfer point. Follow the purple signs, and mention your connection time at the desk — they can fast-track you.
lines.zh: 需要，在中转处。跟着紫色指示牌走，在柜台说明您的中转时间，他们可以帮您走快速通道。

lines.en: That is a relief. And if I miss it, what are my options?
lines.zh: 那我就放心了。万一没赶上，我有什么选择？

lines.en: You would be rebooked on the next available flight at no charge, since the delay was ours.
lines.zh: 因为延误是我们造成的，您会被免费改签到下一个有位的航班。

lines.en: Could you note my seat preference now, just in case? Aisle, towards the front.
lines.zh: 能不能现在先记下我的座位偏好，以防万一？靠走道，靠前一点。

lines.en: Noted. Here is your boarding pass. Gate B22 — boarding closes twenty minutes before departure.
lines.zh: 记下了。这是您的登机牌。B22 登机口，起飞前 20 分钟停止登机。

lines.en: Thank you. One more thing — is there anywhere to grab a quick coffee on the way?
lines.zh: 谢谢。还有一件事——路上有地方能快速买杯咖啡吗？

lines.en: There is a kiosk right past security. Honestly, with fifty minutes, I would skip it.
lines.zh: 过了安检就有个小店。不过说实话，只有 50 分钟的话，我建议您别去了。

dialogs.title: Explaining What You Do at a Dinner Party
dialogs.zhTitle: 在饭局上解释你到底是做什么的
dialogs.goal: 练习用非专业语言介绍专业工作，这是最难也最有用的能力。

lines.en: So what do you actually do? Something with market research?
lines.zh: 你到底是做什么的？跟市场调研有关？

lines.en: Sort of. I work on how products feel — taste, texture, smell — and why people prefer one over another.
lines.zh: 算是吧。我研究产品给人的感受——味道、质地、气味——以及人们为什么更偏爱其中一个。

lines.en: Wait, that is a real job? Who pays for that?
lines.zh: 等等，这是个真实存在的职业？谁会为这个付钱？

lines.en: Anyone who makes something you put in your mouth or on your skin. If two products cost the same, the one that feels right wins.
lines.zh: 任何做入口或上脸产品的公司。两个产品价格一样，感觉对的那个就赢了。

lines.en: Give me an example.
lines.zh: 举个例子。

lines.en: Sure. Think about the sound a jar makes when you first open it. That pop is engineered, and it makes the food taste fresher.
lines.zh: 好。想想第一次拧开一个罐子时的声音。那声"啵"是设计出来的，它会让食物尝起来更新鲜。

lines.en: You are telling me I have been manipulated by a lid.
lines.zh: 你是说我一直在被一个盖子操纵。

lines.en: I would say informed by a lid. Your brain uses every clue it can get, and sound is a very cheap clue.
lines.zh: 我会说是被一个盖子"告知"了。你的大脑会用上一切能拿到的线索，而声音是最廉价的一种。

lines.en: Does knowing all this ruin it for you?
lines.zh: 知道这些会不会让你失去乐趣？

lines.en: Occasionally. But mostly it does the opposite — it turns an ordinary Tuesday breakfast into something worth paying attention to.
lines.zh: 偶尔会。但大多数时候是反过来的——它让一个普通周二的早餐变成值得留意的东西。

keys.en: the one that feels right wins

keys.zh: 被操纵 / 被告知（一组有分寸感的对比）

dialogs.title: Pushing Back on an Impossible Timeline
dialogs.zhTitle: 拒绝一个不可能的排期
dialogs.goal: 练习职场中"有边界感但不对抗"的英文表达。

lines.en: We need the consumer test results by the fifteenth. Can you make that work?
lines.zh: 我们需要在 15 号前拿到消费者测试结果。你能做到吗？

lines.en: Let me walk you through what fifteenth would require, and then you can decide.
lines.zh: 我先带你过一遍 15 号意味着什么，然后你来决定。

lines.en: Okay.
lines.zh: 好。

lines.en: Recruitment alone is eight working days for this profile. That leaves two days for fieldwork and one for analysis.
lines.zh: 光是招募��类人群就要 8 个工作日。剩下 2 天做执行，1 天做分析。

lines.en: Could we shorten recruitment?
lines.zh: 招募能压缩吗？

lines.en: We could, but then we take whoever is available, and 'whoever is available' is a real bias, not a rounding error.
lines.zh: 可以，但那样我们只能要"谁有空要谁"，而"谁有空"是一个真实的偏差，不是舍入误差。

lines.en: What would you propose?
lines.zh: 你的建议是？

lines.en: Two options. A directional read on the fifteenth with a clear health warning, or a defensible result on the twenty-second.
lines.zh: 两个选项。15 号给一个方向性判断，并附明确的局限说明；或者 22 号给一个经得起挑战的结论。

lines.en: The steering committee meets on the eighteenth.
lines.zh: 指导委员会 18 号开会。

lines.en: Then take the directional read, and let me write the caveat slide myself. If someone quotes it out of context in a board deck, we both pay for it.
lines.zh: 那就用方向性判断，但局限说明那页让我自己写。如果有人把它断章取义放进董事会材料，我们两个都要付代价。

lines.en: Deal.
lines.zh: 成交。

keys.zh: 方向性判断（非定论性结论）
不是可以忽略的小误差

dialogs.title: A Room With a Problem
dialogs.goal: 练习礼貌而坚定的投诉与协商。

lines.en: Hi, I checked in about an hour ago into 704. I am afraid the room is not going to work.
lines.zh: 你好，我大约一小时前入住 704。恐怕这个房间不太行。

lines.en: I am sorry to hear that. May I ask what the issue is?
lines.zh: 很抱歉。方便问一下是什么问题吗？

lines.en: There is a persistent smell of damp, and the air conditioning is quite loud. I have an early start tomorrow.
lines.zh: 有一股持续的潮味，空调也挺吵。我明天要早起。

lines.en: Let me see what else we have. We are fairly full tonight.
lines.zh: 我看看还有什么房。今晚我们几乎满房。

lines.en: I appreciate that. I am not asking for an upgrade — just somewhere quiet and dry.
lines.zh: 我理解。我不是要求升级——只想要一个安静干燥的房间。

lines.en: I can offer you 1102. It is a similar layout, higher floor, away from the lift shaft.
lines.zh: 我可以给您 1102。户型相近，楼层更高，远离电梯井。

lines.en: That sounds much better. Could someone help me move the bags?
lines.zh: 那好多了。能安排人帮我搬一下行李吗？

lines.en: Of course. And I will note a late checkout on your booking for the inconvenience.
lines.zh: 当然。另外我会在您的订单上备注延迟退房，作为对不便的补偿。

lines.en: That is very kind — thank you for sorting it out so quickly.
lines.zh: 太贴心了——谢谢你这么快就处理好。

lines.en: You are most welcome. I will have the bellman bring up your new key shortly.
lines.zh: 不客气。我会让行李员马上把新房卡送上去。

lines.en: Perfect. I will head up now and get settled. Thanks again for your help.
lines.zh: 太好了。我现在就上去安顿。再次感谢你的帮助。

keys.en: I am not asking for an upgrade
keys.zh: 我并不是要求升级（降低对抗感）

dialogs.title: Small Talk at a Conference Coffee Break
dialogs.zhTitle: 会议茶歇上的专业闲聊
dialogs.goal: 练习从寒暄自然过渡到有价值的专业交流。

lines.en: That last session was a bit of a sales pitch, was it not?
lines.zh: 刚那场基本就是个推销吧？

lines.en: A little. Though the bit about implicit measurement was worth staying for.
lines.zh: 有一点。不过关于内隐测量的那一段还是值得留下来听的。

lines.en: Are you on the client side or agency?
lines.zh: 你是甲方还是乙方？

lines.en: Client side — I look after sensory and consumer insights for a personal care portfolio.
lines.zh: 甲方——我负责一个个护品类组合的感官与消费者洞察。

lines.en: Then you must be dealing with the AI question constantly.
lines.zh: 那你肯定天天在面对 AI 那个问题。

lines.en: Constantly. My working position is that AI is excellent before fieldwork and dangerous after it.
lines.zh: 天天。我目前的立场是：AI 在田野之前很好用，在田野之后很危险。

lines.en: That is a neat way of putting it. Where do you draw the line exactly?
lines.zh: 这个说法很精炼。你具体在哪里划这条线？

lines.en: Anything that generates hypotheses, yes. Anything that generates respondents, no.
lines.zh: 任何用来生成假设的，可以。任何用来生成受访者的，不行。

lines.en: I might steal that for my next steering group.
lines.zh: 我下次开指导会可能要借用一下这句。

lines.en: Please do. Are you around for the afternoon panel? I would be curious what you make of it.
lines.zh: 尽管用。你下午的圆桌还在吗？我挺想听听你怎么看。

keys.en: a bit of a sales pitch
where do you draw the line

dialogs.title: Moderating a Focus Group
dialogs.zhTitle: 主持一场焦点小组访谈
dialogs.goal: 练习在焦点小组中保持中立、追问而不引导、妥善处理冷场与分歧。

lines.en: Let's start simple — when you first tasted this, what was the very first thing that came to mind?
lines.zh: 咱们从简单处开始——你第一口尝到时，最先冒出来的念头是什么？

lines.en: It felt… clean? Like, not heavy on the tongue.
lines.zh: 感觉……很干净？就是说，舌头上不厚重。

lines.en: Clean — can you stay with that word for a second? What makes it feel clean versus, say, watery?
lines.zh: “干净”——你能就这个词再多说一点吗？它和所谓“寡淡”的区别在哪？

lines.en: For me clean means no aftertaste. Watery would be thin and forgettable.
lines.zh: 对我来说干净就是没有余味。寡淡则是单薄、喝完就忘了。

lines.en: Good distinction. Anyone feel something different in the aftertaste?
lines.zh: 这个区分很好。有人对余味有不同感受吗？

lines.en: There's a slight bitterness at the end. Not bad, just… present.
lines.zh: 尾段有一点苦。不讨厌，就是……存在感。

lines.en: Noted — a late bitterness. And does that bitterness make you want to take another sip, or stop?
lines.zh: 记下了——尾段苦。这种苦是让你想再喝一口，还是想停下？

lines.en: Actually it makes me curious. I'd go again.
lines.zh: 其实它让我有点好奇。我会再喝。

lines.en: Curious is interesting. So the bitterness isn't a reject signal here?
lines.zh: “好奇”这个点有意思。所以这里的苦并不是拒绝信号？

lines.en: No, it feels intentional. Like the product knows what it's doing.
lines.zh: 不是，它感觉是刻意的。像产品心里有数。

keys.en: first thing that came to mind

dialogs.title: Ordering at a Café
dialogs.goal: 掌握点单、定制规格、堂食外带与确认等待时间的日常高频表达。

lines.en: Hi! What can I get for you?
lines.zh: 您好！要点点什么？

lines.en: Could I get a medium flat white, please? With oat milk if you have it.
lines.zh: 麻烦来一杯中杯澳白，可以的话用燕麦奶。

lines.en: Sure — oat milk, medium flat white. Anything to eat?
lines.zh: 好的——燕麦奶，中杯澳白。要配点吃的吗？

lines.en: Maybe one of those almond croissants. Is it still warm?
lines.zh: 来一个那个杏仁可颂吧。现在还是热的吗？

lines.en: Just came out of the oven. Want it heated a little more?
lines.zh: 刚出炉。要再加热一下吗？

lines.en: That'd be great, thank you. And could I get that to stay, not takeaway?
lines.zh: 那太好了，谢谢。这杯我要堂食，不要外带。

lines.en: For here. Name for the cup?
lines.zh: 堂食。杯子写什么名字？

lines.en: It's Echo. How long should I expect to wait?
lines.zh: 写 Echo。大概要等多久？

lines.en: About four minutes — I'll bring it over to your table.
lines.zh: 大概四分钟——我给你送到座位上。

lines.en: Perfect, thanks so much.
lines.zh: 太好了，非常感谢。

dialogs.title: Negotiating a Specification With a Supplier
dialogs.zhTitle: 与供应商谈一份感官规格
dialogs.goal: 练习就感官规格、批次公差与交付节奏与供应商沟通，守住品质底线。

lines.en: So you want the sweetness capped at level 3 on your scale?
lines.zh: 所以你们希望甜度上限压在你们量表的 3 级？

lines.en: Level 3, and critically — no more than a half-step variance between batches.
lines.zh: 3 级，而且关键是——批次之间波动不能超过半级。

lines.en: Half a step is tight. That means we re-calibrate the line every run.
lines.zh: 半级很紧。那意味着每批我们都要重新校准产线。

lines.en: I understand the cost. But the consumer test showed anything above 3.5 drops purchase intent.
lines.zh: 成本我理解。但消费者测试显示，超过 3.5 购买意向就掉。

lines.en: Fair. What if we hold 3.0 to 3.3 and flag anything outside?
lines.zh: 合理。那我们控制在 3.0 到 3.3，超出的做标记，行吗？

lines.en: That works, as long as the flag triggers a hold, not a shipment.
lines.zh: 可以，前提是标记触发的是“扣留”，不是“发货”。

lines.en: Agreed — out-of-band goes to quarantine, not the truck.
lines.zh: 同意——超范围的进待检区，不上车。

lines.en: And lead time? We can't promise the same volume if batches fail.
lines.zh: 那交期呢？如果批次出问题，我们给不了同样产量。

lines.en: We'll build in a 10% buffer stock. You get first refusal on it.
lines.zh: 我们会留 10% 缓冲库存。你们有优先调配权。

lines.en: Good. Let's put the tolerance in writing before pilot.
lines.zh: 好。试点前我们把公差写进合同。

dialogs.title: Getting Directions on the Street
dialogs.goal: 掌握问路、确认距离、交通方式切换与表达感谢的实用句型。

lines.en: Excuse me, is the metro station far from here?
lines.zh: 打扰一下，地铁站离这儿远吗？

lines.en: Which one? There are two within walking distance.
lines.zh: 哪个站？步行范围内有两个。

lines.en: The one near the museum — line 4, I think.
lines.zh: 博物馆旁边那个——应该是 4 号线。

lines.en: That's about a ten-minute walk, straight down this street, then left at the church.
lines.zh: 走过去大概十分钟，沿这条街一直走，到教堂左转。

lines.en: Straight, then left at the church. And is it signposted?
lines.zh: 一直走，教堂左转。那儿有路牌指示吗？

lines.en: Mostly. But the sign's small — look up, not at the shops.
lines.zh: 基本有。但牌子小——抬头看，别盯店铺。

lines.en: Got it. Could I take a bus instead, if I get lost?
lines.zh: 明白了。万一迷路，我能坐公交吗？

lines.en: Bus 11 stops right there. But walking's quicker at this hour.
lines.zh: 11 路公交就在那儿停。不过这会儿走路更快。

lines.en: Perfect, I'll walk. Thank you, you saved me.
lines.zh: 太好了，我走过去。谢谢你，帮了大忙。

lines.en: No problem — enjoy the museum.
lines.zh: 不客气——博物馆好好玩。

dialogs.title: Scheduling a Meeting by Email
dialogs.goal: 练习礼貌提议时间、协调多人日程、提前同步议程与跟进。

lines.en: Hi Mark, hoping to sync on the Q3 research plan — do you have 30 minutes next week?
lines.zh: Mark 你好，想就三季度研究计划对齐一下——下周你有 30 分钟吗？

lines.en: Wednesday looks open. Morning your time?
lines.zh: 周三好像有空。你那边上午？

lines.en: Wednesday 10am works. Should we include Lena from insights?
lines.zh: 周三上午十点可以。要把洞察部的 Lena 也拉上吗？

lines.en: Yes, she owns the consumer data. Send the invite and I'll add her.
lines.zh: 要，消费数据是她负责的。你发邀约，我来加她。

lines.en: Done. I'll share the agenda beforehand so we don't wander.
lines.zh: 发了。我会提前发议程，免得跑题。

lines.en: Please do — last time we spent 20 minutes on the wrong slide.
lines.zh: 务必——上次我们拿错幻灯片耗了 20 分钟。

lines.en: Noted. I'll keep it to three points: scope, timeline, owners.
lines.zh: 记下了。我控制三个点：范围、时间线、责任人。

lines.en: That's the Mark I like. Anything you need from me before?
lines.zh: 这才对味。会前你需要我做什么？

lines.en: Just your take on the budget ceiling. I don't want to over-promise.
lines.zh: 就你对预算上限的看法。我不想过度承诺。

lines.en: I'll send a one-liner by Tuesday. Talk Wednesday.
lines.zh: 周二前我发一句话给你。周三聊。
